text: Great, thank you. So just in terms of our update tonight, again, thanks everybody for joining us virtually. We are going to try to introduce some more Roberts rules, as we can see. So today, there are 175,915 confirmed cases of COVID in New Jersey, with 644 still under investigation. The county has 16,537 cases, and Westfield reported no new cases yesterday, but they did report 12 new cases today, bringing our total to 325 for my update on Sunday. I know the recent upward trend over the last two weeks is not news to most of you, and I will address it in more detail shortly. But I also am very saddened to report that we have reports of additional fatality, an 82-year-old male associated with a long-term care facility. It is a death that occurred back in May, but it was only now reported to us due to an error in the lab's reporting system. So regardless of the timing, we just want to remember and acknowledge that there is another life that's tragically lost. I think that brings us up to 43, and we keep this resident and his family in our thoughts. There's some updates, you know, in terms of Governor Murphy announced additional 14-day quarantine periods for additional states, bringing a total up to now 22. The good news is New Jersey is one of only 12 that's meeting its current testing targets, and hopefully that will continue. And anybody that's starting to get back into commuting mode, the governor signed an executive order yesterday lifting the 50 percent capacity limits the first enforced on New Jersey transit. Base coverings are always required. And very importantly, and hopefully we've let all of our businesses know, that Union County has launched a COVID-19 relief grant program. It's for small businesses that have been impacted by the health emergency, up to two million dollars in CARES Act relief funds, and so grants up to $20,000 for small businesses of 25 or less employees. So there's information available on our website for how you can apply. Very importantly, yesterday I participated in a Zoom call with New Jersey Transit, along with other members of the RVL Mayor's Alliance and the Raritan Valley Rail Coalition, and they presented the results of the RVL one-seat ride feasibility study that was approved by the legislature back in December. So I have to say we were pretty disappointed with their findings, not completely surprised by it, and we found their findings were limited in both the options they presented and the ridership data that they had considered. So it concluded that there is additional capacity to add trains during the off-peak shoulder period, but it would take a long time and a lot of money to do so, which didn't feel credible to most of us that were listening. So as disappointed as we were, it is just the beginning of a political legislative process, and it's going to evolve as the transit situation becomes more certain post-COVID. I spoke to Congressman Tom Malinowski yesterday, who's also advocating at the governor's office, and even New Jersey Transit acknowledges this is just the beginning of the conversation, by no means the end of the conversation. So stay tuned for updates and just know that the RVL mayors certainly are not going to give up our fight for equitable service. I want to let you know too the Westfield Memorial Library has postponed its limited reopening that's been scheduled for yesterday, just in light of the recent uptick in COVID numbers, just out of abundance of caution. So they will continue to provide curbside service for now with their expanded hours, so details to come as things move forward. Tonight we're doing something very exciting on the agenda. We are taking our first step in the implementation of the strategic parks plan, and the council is voting on a resolution to award a contract for planning and design services for the development of master recreation plan on the Edison school property, which includes two turf fields. So the plan is to ultimately determine what is the best ultimate use of the property. They're going to be talking to all the stakeholders, not only the sports leagues, but also the school administrators and sports folks, and ultimately come up with a real plan with what it could be and what the actual cost would be. So we're very excited about moving that step forward. There's also another thing tonight that we have on ordinance on first reading out of the code review and town property committee, and we'll be amending a certain section of our land use ordinance relating to the definitions of pet care facilities, so we can expand the permitted uses in certain zone districts, particularly our downtown. So we're always trying to make sure that our land use allowances and zoning allowances evolve with I think current trends, and certainly I think pet care and and so forth seems to be a very big emerging trend. I want to take, we have joining with us tonight is our regional health director Megan Avalon, and before I talk and address the recent COVID trend, I want to hand it off to Megan and hear it from the horse's mouth, if you will, about what's going on, what we're seeing, and any other context that she can provide. So with that, I'll hand it off to you, Megan. Thank you, Mayor.

The other thing that we're getting lots of questions about is about if you know that you were in contact with somebody who tests positive, should you run out and get a test immediately, right? There seems to be a lot of questions about when to test if you think you've been exposed, and certainly the health department encourages testing for residents who think they've been exposed, but that does not take the place of the quarantine period. So we know that especially with COVID-19, you can incubate the virus for up to 14 days.
